\chapter{More Everyday Verbs}
\label{ch:te-more-verbs}
\hlchaptermodality{43}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can tell someone to come, sit, stand and give in Telugu.}

Complete TE-C43-give and say all four verbs in order.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[rā]{\te{రా} (rā) — come}

\label{lesson:TE-C43-come}



\begin{quote}
A short run of everyday verbs, one at a time.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \te{రా}}
\textbf{\te{రా}} (\emph{rā}) — \textquotedblleft{}come\textquotedblright{}.

The bare command, and one of the shortest words in the language: a single syllable that is a complete sentence.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more everyday action. Three more follow, and each reuses the ones before it.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{rā}
  \item it again, to someone standing in a doorway
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \te{రా} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}come\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[kūrcō]{\te{కూర్చో} (kūrcō) — sit}

\label{lesson:TE-C43-sit}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{rā} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \te{కూర్చో}}
\textbf{\te{కూర్చో}} (\emph{kūrcō}) — \textquotedblleft{}sit\textquotedblright{}.

A command you will hear on entering any home, usually before anything else is said.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more everyday action. Three more follow, and each reuses the ones before it.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{kūrcō}
  \item it again, to someone standing in a doorway
  \item it after \emph{rā}, so the two sit together
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \te{కూర్చో} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}sit\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[nilcō]{\te{నిల్చో} (nilcō) — stand}

\label{lesson:TE-C43-stand}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{kūrcō} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \te{నిల్చో}}
\textbf{\te{నిల్చో}} (\emph{nilcō}) — \textquotedblleft{}stand\textquotedblright{}.

Its pair. Telugu, like the other Dravidian languages, makes the bare stem do the work of a command with nothing added.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more everyday action. Three more follow, and each reuses the ones before it.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{nilcō}
  \item it again, to someone standing in a doorway
  \item it after \emph{kūrcō}, so the two sit together
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \te{నిల్చో} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}stand\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ivvu]{\te{ఇవ్వు} (ivvu) — give}

\label{lesson:TE-C43-give}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{nilcō} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \te{ఇవ్వు}}
\textbf{\te{ఇవ్వు}} (\emph{ivvu}) — \textquotedblleft{}give\textquotedblright{}.

The everyday 'give'. Softening it is done with a separate politeness word rather than by changing the verb.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more everyday action. That closes the run: four everyday actions, each met on its own.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{ivvu}
  \item it again, to someone standing in a doorway
  \item it after \emph{nilcō}, so the two sit together
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \te{ఇవ్వు} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}give\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
